options: An ordered dictionary mapping each layer's name to its learned tensor values, with no class or architecture code
A compiled binary of the model ready to run without PyTorch
A list of all the input/output shapes used during training
The optimizer's hyperparameters only
questions.explain: state_dict() returns an OrderedDict of parameter/buffer names to tensors — just the learned numbers, which is why it's portable and the recommended thing to save.

questions.q: Why is saving model.state_dict() preferred over torch.save(model, ...) (saving the whole object)?
options: state_dict() files are always smaller

The whole-model approach pickles a reference to the class definition, so loading later requires that exact class to be importable in the same way; state_dict only needs the numbers plus an already-constructed model instance
state_dict() is the only method that works on GPU-trained models
There is no real difference; both are equally recommended
questions.explain: Saving the whole model object ties the checkpoint to your current class definition and import structure, making it fragile to refactors. state_dict avoids this by storing only tensor values, loaded into a model you construct yourself.

questions.q: After loading a trained model's weights for inference, what should you call before running predictions, and why?
options: model.train(), to make sure gradients are enabled
model.eval(), because layers like dropout and batch norm behave differently in training vs. inference, and skipping this silently changes predictions
model.reset(), to clear the loaded weights
Nothing extra is needed; loading already sets the correct mode
questions.explain: model.eval() switches layers such as Dropout and BatchNorm into their inference behavior. Forgetting it doesn't raise an error — it just produces worse or inconsistent predictions, making it an easy silent bug.

questions.q: Why would you include the optimizer's state_dict in a training checkpoint, not just the model's?
options: The optimizer's state_dict is required for torch.save to work at all
Optimizers like Adam track per-parameter running statistics (e.g. momentum); without restoring that state, resuming training restarts those statistics from zero, which can disrupt training
It makes the checkpoint file smaller
It is not useful; only the model's state_dict ever matters
questions.explain: Stateful optimizers accumulate per-parameter statistics over training. Omitting the optimizer state from a checkpoint means those statistics reset to zero on resume, which can cause a visible disruption in training dynamics.

questions.q: What is required in your code before calling model.load_state_dict(torch.load("weights.pt"))?
options: Nothing; load_state_dict reconstructs the model architecture automatically
An already-constructed instance of the same model class whose parameter names and shapes match the saved state_dict
The optimizer must be constructed and trained first
The GPU must be available
questions.explain: load_state_dict only copies tensor values into an existing model's parameters by matching names/shapes — it does not build the architecture, so you must construct the model class yourself first.
